title: A gathering of water
text:
The rivers of South America as one connected network. Each line is a stretch of river, and each stretch passes its water on to exactly one next stretch, until it reaches the coast or an inland ending. Touch a river to follow its water down (the dark line) and to light the tributaries that gather into it. Brush a finger along the lines to follow many in turn.

There is no route to finish. Every line has somewhere to go.

sections.title: What the lines are
sections.text:
The connections come from RiverATLAS v1.0, a river network derived from elevation data. Only larger channels are drawn: reaches with at least 500 km² of land upstream, plus their downstream connections. That keeps 218,146 of the 1,620,963 South American reaches, merged here into 18,159 stretches between junctions. The great rivers show from far away, the smaller ones as you come closer. A touch snaps to the nearest line drawn.

The tributaries lit above a touch are the ones retained here, not every stream, and not a surveyed catchment boundary.

sections.title: What is measured
sections.text:
Distances are rounded sums of mapped channel lengths along the network, not straight lines. The first, partial stretch is estimated along its simplified line. Areas are RiverATLAS's land upstream of a stretch's lower end, and at its outlet for a whole system.

The moving glint shows only which way the water goes: its speed is invented. This is not a simulation of rainfall, travel time, present flow, flood risk or navigability.

sections.title: The limits of a line
sections.text: A branching dataset gives each reach one downstream connection. Real rivers can divide, shift, flood, flow through wetlands, and be changed by people. The Casiquiare, for example, links the Orinoco and Amazon systems; this simplified tree cannot express that connection. An inland ending does not mean an empty landscape.

sections.title: Names
sections.text: These rivers are lived places, with many names and meanings. The few river and town names here are orientation aids. A river's name marks a mapped channel near a named place, and the words at the foot say the water passes it only when the network's links lead through that very stretch. A system's name, such as the Amazon system, is given to every stretch that drains to the same outlet. A drainage network cannot stand in for the lives, histories, or knowledge of the people along it.

sections.title: How it was made
sections.text: The study's build selected the larger reaches from the RiverATLAS download, merged chains without a retained tributary, simplified the lines to 0.006° and rounded them to 0.001°, never inventing a connection; its source files' checksums travel with the data. For the globe the lines are simplified further, keeping every link, length and area. The coasts, relief and borders are the globe's own.
